check.q: A frog hops 3 each time from 0: 3, 6, 9 ... Use a counter or draw the hops. What number does it land on next?
A bunny starts at 1 and hops 3 each time: 1, 4, 7 ... Will it land on 20? How do you know?
check.a: No. It lands on 19, then 22, so it jumps over 20. (Keep hopping, or notice it only lands on numbers that are 1 more than a 3s number.)

invest.title: What if we change the hops?
invest.q: Now change frog 2 to hops of 4, then 5, then 6, and do it again each time. What stays the same? What changes?
invest.model: Both land on: with 3s 6, 12, 18, 24, 30; with 4s 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28 (every landing of frog 2, because 4 is a number in the 2s); with 5s 10, 20, 30; with 6s 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. Stays the same: 0 is always shared, and the shared numbers always form a pattern with equal jumps. Changes: the size of that jump (6, 4, 10, 6) and how many numbers are shared. Look for: both lists written out, a systematic check, and a reason why the 4s frog shares every landing (4 = 2 + 2). Accept any correct noticing.
invest.first: Frog 1 hops in 2s from 0. Frog 2 hops in 3s from 0. Write the numbers up to 30 that BOTH frogs land on.

check.q: There are 10 sweets. 7 are red and the rest are green. Use counters or draw them. How many are green?
Ali has 7 red counters and 5 blue counters. Mei has 6 red counters and 6 blue counters. Who has more counters, or do they have the same? How do you know?
check.a: The same: 12 each. (7 + 5 = 12 and 6 + 6 = 12. Ali's 7 is 1 more than Mei's 6, but his 5 is 1 less than her 6.)

invest.title: Is it always true?
invest.q: Mei says: "When two numbers make 10, they are both odd or both even." Is Mei always right? Now test the pairs that make 20. Why do you think it works?
invest.model: Yes. All 11 pairs from 0 + 10 to 10 + 0 are both odd or both even (1 + 9, 3 + 7 ... and 0 + 10, 2 + 8 ...); the same holds for all 21 pairs that make 20. Reason (accept child language): when one number goes up by 1 the other goes down by 1, so both change from odd to even together. Or: an odd and an even always make an odd total, never 10 or 20. Look for: testing every pair (not 2 or 3), writing them in order, and a reason that is more than "it just works".
invest.first: Write all the pairs that make 10, from 0 + 10 and 1 + 9 down to 10 + 0. Look at each pair. Are both numbers odd, both even, or one of each?

check.q: 1 picture = 1 child. Count the pictures: how many children chose blue? (Red has 7 pictures, blue has 5 and green has 3.)
How many MORE children chose red than green?
check.a: 4 more (7 − 3). Compare the two rows: do not add.

invest.title: What if we change the key?
invest.q: Now draw it again with 1 picture = 2 children. What stays the same? What changes? Could you use 1 picture = 3 children? Why or why not?
invest.model: With 1 picture = 2 children: Cats 2 pictures, Dogs 3, Fish 1. Stays the same: 12 children in all, dogs still win, fish still last, the same number of children chose each. Changes: the number of pictures (it halves). A key of 3 does not work: 4 and 2 are not in the 3s, so we would need part of a picture. A key only works when every count is in its counting pattern (here the keys 1 and 2 work). Look for: correct rows, the key written on the graph, and a reason that talks about counting in 2s or 3s.
invest.first: Draw a picture graph with 1 picture = 1 child: Cats 4, Dogs 6, Fish 2.

check.q: Beads repeat: red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue ... Draw or thread the next 3 beads.
check.a: Red, blue, blue. The pattern is red, blue, blue again and again.

check.q: Same pattern. What colour is the 12th bead? How do you know?
check.a: Blue. The pattern repeats every 3 beads, so the 3rd, 6th, 9th and 12th beads end a repeat, and each repeat ends with blue.

invest.title: Is it always true?
invest.q: Mei says: "In a pattern that repeats every 3 shapes, place 30 is the same shape as place 3." Test Mei on places 6 and 9, then on place 30. Is she always right? What about a pattern that repeats every 4 shapes: which places match place 4?
invest.model: Yes, always. Any pattern that repeats every 3 shapes has the same shape in places 3, 6, 9, 12 ... 30 (we say these when we count in 3s, so each one ends a repeat). For a pattern that repeats every 4 shapes, places 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 ... match place 4. Look for: a real 3-shape pattern drawn to place 9, testing before agreeing, and the link to counting in 3s (or 4s). Extra: ask "Which place matches place 1 in a 3-shape pattern?" (places 4, 7, 10 ... 31).
invest.first: Draw your own pattern of 3 shapes that repeats (for example circle, square, triangle, circle, square, triangle ...) up to place 9.

check.q: Put 8 counters in a cup. Add 3 more. How many counters are in the cup now?
I think of a number. I add 3. Then I add 4. I get 12. What is my number?
check.a: 5. Undo the last step first: 12 − 4 = 8, then undo the first step: 8 − 3 = 5. Check: 5 + 3 = 8, 8 + 4 = 12.

invest.title: Is it always true?
invest.q: Mei says: "OUT is always the same as IN." Test one number you choose. Is Mei always right? Now change the machine: add 6, then take away 4. What happens to every number? Why?
invest.model: Yes: adding 6 then taking away 6 puts every number back (the steps undo each other). With add 6 then take away 4: 3 gives 5, 10 gives 12, 25 gives 27, so OUT is always 2 more than IN, because the machine really adds 6 − 4 = 2. Look for: four or more tests, a table, and an explanation using "undo" or "6 then back 6". Extra: "Design a machine that always gives 3 less."
invest.first: A number machine adds 6 and then takes away 6. Try IN = 3, 10 and 25. What comes OUT each time?

check.q: Ben has a 20¢ coin, a 10¢ coin and a 5¢ coin. Draw them. Can he pay 25¢ exactly?
Show one way to make 15¢ with 5¢ and 10¢ coins. Can you find a different way?
check.a: 10¢ + 5¢, and 5¢ + 5¢ + 5¢. Those are the only two ways.

invest.title: What if we take a coin away?
invest.q: Which amounts from 5¢ to 50¢ (5¢, 10¢, 15¢ ... 50¢) can you NOT make with the 10¢, 20¢ and 50¢ coins? What do those amounts have in common? Why?
invest.model: You cannot make 5¢, 15¢, 25¢, 35¢ or 45¢. You can make 10¢, 20¢, 30¢, 40¢ and 50¢. The amounts you cannot make all end in 5: every coin left ends in 0, so any total ends in 0. Extension: put the 10¢ coin away instead (keep 5¢, 20¢, 50¢): now every amount from 5¢ to 50¢ can be made (e.g. 10¢ = 5¢ + 5¢). Look for: using real coins, a list of what works and what fails, and a reason about last digits (accept "all the coins end in 0").
invest.first: Our coins are 5¢, 10¢, 20¢ and 50¢. Put the 5¢ coin away. Use your coins to make 10¢, then 20¢, then 15¢.

tx.label: T5
tx.q: Dollars! We also have $1 coins and $2, $5, $10 and $50 notes.
subs: A toy costs $17. Pay exactly with the fewest notes and coins.
Mei has one $50 note and two $10 notes. A bicycle costs $65 and a helmet costs $8. Does she have enough money for both? Explain.
tx.a: (a) $10 + $5 + $2 (3 pieces).  (b) No. She has $50 + $10 + $10 = $70. The bicycle and helmet cost $65 + $8 = $73. She is $3 short.

check.q: Draw a triangle. Count its straight sides and count its corners.
A shape has 9 corners. How many straight sides does it have? How do you know?
check.a: 9. A shape has as many straight sides as it has corners.

invest.title: Find all the shapes
invest.q: How many different shapes can you make with 3 squares? Turning or flipping a shape does not make a new one. Draw each shape. Then try with 4 squares. Use paper squares or counters to help.
invest.model: 3 squares: 2 shapes (a straight line of 3 and a bent shape, like an L). 4 squares: 5 shapes (a line of 4, an L, a T, an S or Z, and a big square). Look for: whole sides touching (not corners only), noticing that a turned shape is the same shape, and a way to know when there are no more (start with a line, then move one square). The 4-square task is the extension: accept 3 or 4 shapes with praise for the method.
invest.first: Join 3 squares so that whole sides touch. Draw one shape you can make.

check.q: Ben is shorter than Cara. Cara is shorter than Dev. Draw them in a line. Who is in the middle?
check.a: Cara. The order from shortest is Ben, Cara, Dev.

check.q: Which number does NOT belong: 4, 8, 12, 15? Give a reason. Can you find a different reason?
check.a: 15 (it is not in the 4s; it is the only odd number; it is the only one that ends in 5). Accept any reasoned answer.
check.short: 15: not in the 4s, or the only odd one

invest.title: Find all the ways
invest.q: Write ALL the different orders they can stand in. How do you know you have them all? Now add a clue: "Ali is not first." How many orders are left? Make up your own clue so that only ONE order is left.
invest.model: There are 6 orders: Ali Mei Ben, Ali Ben Mei, Mei Ali Ben, Mei Ben Ali, Ben Ali Mei, Ben Mei Ali. With "Ali is not first" 4 are left. Clues that leave exactly one: "Ali is in front of Ben and Ben is in front of Mei" (Ali, Ben, Mei), or "Mei is first and Ali is not last" (Mei, Ali, Ben). Look for: a systematic list (fix who is first, then list the other two) and the reason "each of 3 children can be first and then 2 orders follow". Accept any clue that leaves exactly one order after the child tests it.
invest.first: Ali, Mei and Ben stand in a line. Write one order they can stand in. Now write a different order.

tx.label: T5
subs: I am between 20 and 40. When you count in 2s you say me. When you count in 5s you say me too.
I have 2 digits. When I add my two digits I get 5. I am less than 20.

check.q: Ribbon A is 5 squares long. Ribbon B is 3 squares long. Which ribbon is longer? How many squares longer?
check.a: Ribbon A, by 2 squares (5 − 3). Draw or count the squares.

check.q: Ali measures a table with his pencil and gets 5 pencils. Mei measures the same table with a shorter pencil. Will she count more pencils or fewer pencils? Why?
check.a: More. A shorter pencil covers less, so she needs more of them.
check.short: More: a shorter unit needs more of them

invest.title: Is it always true?
invest.q: Which unit is shorter? Which one gave the bigger number? Ben says: "If I measure the same thing with a SHORTER unit, I always get a BIGGER number." Is Ben right? Guess: if a unit is half as long as a cube, what number would you get for your pencil?
invest.model: Yes, always: more short units are needed to cover the same length. A unit half as long gives double the number (a pencil of 12 cubes is 24 half cubes). Look for: units laid end to end with no gaps, starting at the end of the pencil, both counts written down, and a reason using "shorter unit, more of them". Accept any measured numbers if the shorter unit has the bigger count.
invest.first: Measure your pencil with the cube strip. Write the number. Then measure it with a paper clip (or your finger width). Write the number.

check.q: The pattern is 4, 9, 14, 19 ... Write the next two numbers.
Make 35¢ with exactly 3 coins from 5¢, 10¢, 20¢ and 50¢.

invest.title: What if we change the jump?
invest.q: Now change the jump to 1, 2, 4 and 5 and find each total. What stays the same? What changes? Can you find a shortcut for the total?
invest.model: Totals: jump 1 gives 5 + 6 + 7 = 18; jump 2 gives 21; jump 3 gives 24; jump 4 gives 27; jump 5 gives 30. Stays the same: the first number is 5 and there are always 3 numbers. Changes: the total goes up by 3 each time the jump goes up by 1. Shortcut: the total is 3 times the middle number (3 times 8 = 24), or 15 plus 3 jumps. Look for: a tidy table of jump and total, and any noticing of the +3 pattern. Extra: predict the total for a jump of 10 (45).
invest.first: Three numbers in a row start at 5 and jump by 3: 5, 8, 11. Add them up. What is the total?
